$comment: The run outcome vocabulary, as data, so it is stated once and read twice. events.py reads it at import and asserts every tool outcome has an action; web/src/server generates its types from the same file. Restating it in TypeScript would give a compile-time check at the cost of two statements of one vocabulary drifting silently - the alphabet problem again, and a compile error about a stale copy is worse than a runtime assertion about the real one.

ok.description: declared outputs exist, are non-empty, and detect as the declared type

nonzero_exit.action: look at the data, or the tool

oom.description: killed against the machine class memory cap

precondition_failed.description: an input did not satisfy what the operation requires, so it never ran - the wrong kind of file, not a tool or platform failure

missing_output.description: a declared output is absent or empty, whatever the exit code
missing_output.action: look at the data, or the tool

type_mismatch.description: an output exists but is not the declared type

image_missing.description: the image could not be obtained - infrastructure, not the tool

conformant.description: adapter drafted and passing conform.py, ready for review

needs_review.description: conformant, but with a caveat a human should see - unknown license, or a port that fell back to the Text escape hatch

gave_up.description: could not produce a conformant adapter; the report says what it could not determine. The honest outcome, and far better than a plausible adapter nobody can trust

rejected.description: the run touched files outside its own adapter directory and was discarded. A guardrail trip, not a tool problem

actions.$comment: Outcomes are grouped by what a person does next, not by what went wrong. precondition_failed and oom are both 'no result', but one is fixed by choosing a different file and the other by us; telling someone to wait when they are one dropdown from done is a worse error than not grouping. Adding an outcome without an action is caught by an assertion in events.py, which fired the first time it ran - timeout had none, in both of our tables.
order: look at the data, or the tool

evidence.$comment: timeout is the one outcome whose correct action genuinely depends on the run, so it carries numbers even inside a coarse bucket. '180s budget, 182s elapsed, input 40x the profiling fixture' tells a person which case they are in. The family stays fixed rather than being derived per run - a derived family makes aggregate counts unstable, since 'our problem: 12' would start depending on whether `measured` happened to be populated.
